title: SummaC: Re-Visiting NLI-based Models for Inconsistency Detection in Summarization
research_question: Can natural-language-inference models reliably detect factual inconsistency in summaries if the granularity mismatch between sentence-level NLI training and document-level summarization evaluation is explicitly addressed?
methodology: The authors split source documents and summaries into smaller text blocks and run an NLI model over every source-summary block pair to form an NLI pair matrix. SummaC-ZS aggregates maximum entailment evidence per summary sentence without training, while SummaC-Conv bins the score distributions and learns a small convolutional aggregation layer on a subset of synthetic FactCC training data. Evaluation uses the SummaC Benchmark, which standardizes six existing factual-consistency datasets into binary classification tasks, with balanced accuracy as the primary metric, ROC-AUC as a secondary metric, and bootstrap significance tests against prior systems.

key_findings.finding: Using sentence-level or similarly fine-grained NLI comparisons substantially improves inconsistency detection compared with applying NLI directly to full documents and summaries.
SummaC-Conv achieved 74.4 percent average balanced accuracy on the six-dataset SummaC Benchmark, approximately five absolute points above the strongest reported non-NLI baseline.

Overall improvements of both SummaC variants over prior work were statistically significant under the paper's bootstrap testing procedure, with the stronger significance level reported for SummaC-Conv.
Using the full distribution of sentence-level entailment scores in SummaC-Conv is more robust than relying only on each summary sentence's single maximum entailment score.

NLI architecture and training data materially affect factual-consistency performance, with Transformer-based models and domain-relevant NLI data outperforming the older decomposable-attention setup used in earlier negative results.

The benchmark standardization exposes substantial variation in annotation regimes, class balance and source summarization datasets, rather than assuming that all factuality datasets measure an identical distribution.

limitations: All six benchmark datasets are from news summarization, so performance outside that domain was not established.
Benchmark datasets differ in annotation quality, annotator expertise, labeling schemes and class balance.
Some datasets lacked existing validation/test splits, requiring the authors to construct deterministic splits.
Some benchmark datasets have only one annotator per example, preventing inter-annotator reliability estimates for those datasets.
Sentence-level decomposition can miss evidence requiring cross-sentence or multi-hop reasoning.
The system detects inconsistency but does not itself solve factual correction or guarantee factual summaries.
Performance remains far below perfect consistency detection despite outperforming the compared baselines.
raw_claims: Earlier NLI-based factuality approaches suffered from a mismatch between sentence-level NLI training and document-level summarization inputs.
SummaC represents support using pairwise NLI scores between source and summary text blocks.
SummaC-ZS uses the strongest source-sentence support for each summary sentence and then aggregates across the summary.
SummaC-Conv learns from the distribution of NLI scores rather than depending only on extrema.
The SummaC Benchmark combines six factual-consistency datasets into a common binary classification setup.
Balanced accuracy is used because the component datasets have strongly different class distributions.
SummaC-Conv obtained the highest overall balanced accuracy among the compared methods.
Fine textual granularity generally outperformed full-document NLI evaluation.
The source and quality of NLI training data materially affected downstream consistency detection.
The authors publicly released the SummaC models and standardized benchmark data.
The benchmark is concentrated on news and does not establish performance in other document domains.
